name: Fever in adults
summary: A high temperature is usually 38C (100.4F) or above and is most often caused by a viral infection. It usually gets better on its own within 3 days.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
A stiff neck, pain when looking at bright lights, or a severe headache
Confusion, slurred speech, extreme drowsiness or difficulty waking
Cold, blotchy, pale or blue-tinged skin, lips or tongue
Difficulty breathing, breathing very fast, or chest pain
Not peeing all day, or shivering uncontrollably with feeling very unwell
A seizure (fit)
urgentFlags: A temperature of 40C (104F) or higher
A high temperature with a weakened immune system, such as during chemotherapy
A high temperature after recent travel abroad, especially to an area with malaria
Pain when peeing, pain in your back or side, or a red, hot, swollen area of skin
A high temperature during pregnancy or after recently giving birth
Symptoms getting worse after starting to improve

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu, COVID-19 and stomach bugs are the most common causes.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infections
commonCauses.detail: Urine, chest, skin or throat infections may need antibiotics.

commonCauses.title: Vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: A mild temperature for a day or two after a vaccine is common.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, inflammatory conditions or medicines can cause fever.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids such as water so your pee is pale
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel uncomfortable, following the pack instructions
Wear light clothing and keep the room comfortably cool
Stay at home and avoid contact with others while you have a high temperature
avoid: Cold baths or sponging with cold water, which can make you shiver
Taking paracetamol and combination cold remedies together, which can lead to taking too much paracetamol
Antibiotics left over from a previous illness
seeDoctorIf: Your temperature has lasted more than 3 days
You keep getting high temperatures
You have night sweats or weight loss with a temperature
You are worried about your symptoms

name: Tiredness and fatigue
summary: Feeling tired is very common and is often linked to sleep, stress, diet or a recent illness. Tiredness that lasts weeks without a clear reason is worth checking.
redFlags: Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, a drooping face or slurred speech
Extreme tiredness with chest pain, severe breathlessness or fainting
Extreme drowsiness or confusion with a high temperature
Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life
urgentFlags: Tiredness with vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo
Tiredness with breathlessness, a racing heart or looking very pale
Tiredness with extreme thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss

commonCauses.title: Lifestyle
commonCauses.detail: Not enough sleep, irregular hours, alcohol, caffeine, too little or too much exercise.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or low mood
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain and depression commonly cause exhaustion.

commonCauses.title: Recent infection
commonCauses.detail: Tiredness can last several weeks after viral illnesses such as flu or COVID-19.

commonCauses.title: Anaemia or thyroid problems
commonCauses.detail: Iron deficiency and an underactive thyroid are common, treatable causes.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes, sleep apnoea, chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), medicines, and less commonly cancer.

selfCare: Go to bed and get up at the same time every day
Eat regular, balanced meals and drink enough water
Be active every day, starting gently if needed
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening
Talk to someone or seek support if stress or worry is the cause
avoid: Energy drinks and large amounts of caffeine
Unproven 'energy-boosting' or 'adrenal fatigue' supplements
Napping for long periods during the day
seeDoctorIf: You have felt tired for several weeks without an obvious reason
Tiredness is affecting your daily life
You have also lost weight without trying
You have other symptoms such as heavy periods, night sweats or swollen glands
You snore loudly and stop breathing in your sleep

name: Unexplained weight loss
summary: Losing weight without trying, especially 5% or more of your body weight over 6 to 12 months, should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Weight loss with vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
Weight loss with extreme thirst, peeing a lot, vomiting, fast breathing or confusion
urgentFlags: Weight loss with difficulty swallowing
Weight loss with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Weight loss with being very thirsty and peeing a lot

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or depression
commonCauses.detail: Can reduce appetite and lead to weight loss.

commonCauses.title: Overactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Weight loss with a fast heartbeat, sweating and anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes
commonCauses.detail: Weight loss with thirst, peeing a lot and tiredness.

commonCauses.title: Digestive problems
commonCauses.detail: Coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or other conditions that affect absorption.

commonCauses.title: Cancer or long-term infections
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason unexplained weight loss needs checking.

selfCare: Weigh yourself and record it so you can show the doctor how much you have lost and over what time
Note any other symptoms such as changes in appetite, bowel habit, sweating or tiredness
Eat regular meals and snacks while waiting to be seen
avoid: Waiting to see if it stops
Assuming weight loss is due to stress without being checked
seeDoctorIf: You have lost weight without trying
You have also had a change in bowel habits, night sweats or tiredness
You have a lump anywhere in your body

name: Night sweats
summary: Night sweats are often caused by the menopause, infections, anxiety or medicines. Regular night sweats with weight loss or other symptoms should be checked.
redFlags: Night sweats with confusion, fast breathing or cold, blotchy skin
Sweating with chest pain or breathlessness
urgentFlags: Night sweats with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
Night sweats with coughing up blood
Night sweats after travel abroad

commonCauses.title: Menopause
commonCauses.detail: Hot flushes and night sweats are very common around the menopause.

commonCauses.title: Infections
commonCauses.detail: Flu and other infections; less commonly tuberculosis or HIV.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Stress and worry can cause sweating at night.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol or drugs
commonCauses.detail: Antidepressants, steroids and alcohol are common causes.

commonCauses.title: Lymphoma or other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, night sweats with weight loss and swollen glands.

selfCare: Keep your bedroom cool and use light, breathable bedding
Wear loose cotton nightwear
Cut down on alcohol, caffeine and spicy food, especially in the evening
avoid: Heavy duvets and synthetic bedding
Alcohol before bed
seeDoctorIf: You have regular night sweats that wake you up
You also have a high temperature, weight loss or swollen glands
You have a cough that has lasted more than 3 weeks
Night sweats are affecting your sleep

name: Swollen glands
summary: Swollen glands are usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, such as a cold or sore throat, and normally go down within 2 weeks.
redFlags: Swelling in the neck with difficulty breathing or swallowing
Swollen glands with a rash that does not fade when pressed under a glass
urgentFlags: Swollen glands with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
A gland that is red, hot, very painful or getting bigger quickly

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu and sore throats commonly cause tender glands in the neck.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infections
commonCauses.detail: Throat, tooth, skin or ear infections.

commonCauses.title: Glandular fever
commonCauses.detail: Swollen glands with a sore throat and severe tiredness, often in teenagers and young adults.

commonCauses.title: Lymphoma or other cancers
commonCauses.detail: Less common; usually painless, hard glands that do not go down.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
Check the gland over the next 2 weeks to see if it goes down
avoid: Squeezing or massaging the gland
Antibiotics without a diagnosis
seeDoctorIf: Swollen glands are still there after 2 weeks
A gland feels hard or does not move when you press it
Glands are getting bigger
You also have night sweats, weight loss or a high temperature with no obvious cause

name: Chills and shivering
summary: Shivering and feeling cold are often the body's way of raising its temperature at the start of an infection. Uncontrollable shaking with feeling very unwell can be a sign of sepsis.
redFlags: Shivering uncontrollably with feeling very unwell, confused or very drowsy
Cold, blotchy, pale or blue-tinged skin, lips or tongue
Fast breathing, breathlessness or a very fast heartbeat
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
Not peeing all day
Very low body temperature after being outside in the cold, with confusion or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Shivering with pain when peeing or pain in your back or side
Shivering with a red, hot, swollen area of skin
Shivering with a weakened immune system, such as during chemotherapy
Chills after travel abroad

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Flu and other viruses often cause chills along with a high temperature.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infection
commonCauses.detail: Kidney, chest or skin infections can cause severe shivering (rigors).

commonCauses.title: Cold exposure
commonCauses.detail: Being cold or wet for a long time.

commonCauses.title: Malaria
commonCauses.detail: Chills and fever after visiting an area with malaria, even months later.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use a light blanket while shivering, and remove extra layers once you feel hot
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel unwell, following the pack instructions
Check your temperature and other symptoms regularly
avoid: Piling on lots of blankets if you have a high temperature
Hot baths when feeling faint or very unwell
seeDoctorIf: Chills keep coming back
You have had chills and a temperature for more than 3 days
You also have night sweats or weight loss

name: Dehydration
summary: Dehydration means your body loses more fluid than it takes in. It is common with vomiting, diarrhoea, heat or exercise and can usually be treated by drinking more.
redFlags: Confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Not peeing all day
A fast heartbeat or fast breathing with feeling very unwell
Sunken eyes, cold hands and feet, or blotchy skin in a child
A seizure (fit)
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down
Feeling dizzy or lightheaded when standing that does not go away
Dark pee or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Dehydration in a baby, young child, older person or someone with diabetes or kidney disease

commonCauses.title: Diarrhoea and vomiting
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause, especially in children and older people.

commonCauses.title: Heat and exercise
commonCauses.detail: Sweating a lot in hot weather or during exercise.

commonCauses.title: Fever
commonCauses.detail: A high temperature increases fluid loss.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Alcohol and diuretics make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: High blood sugar
commonCauses.detail: Uncontrolled diabetes causes thirst and peeing a lot.

selfCare: Drink fluids often in small sips, aiming for pale yellow pee
Use oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy if you have diarrhoea or vomiting
Rest somewhere cool
Keep giving breast or formula milk to babies, little and often
avoid: Alcohol and lots of caffeine while dehydrated
Sugary fizzy drinks or undiluted fruit juice if you have diarrhoea
Giving young children sports drinks instead of oral rehydration solution
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not improved after drinking more fluids
You often feel very thirsty
You are peeing a lot or losing weight

name: Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
summary: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes is called jaundice and can be a sign of a problem with the liver, gallbladder or pancreas. It always needs to be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Jaundice with confusion, extreme drowsiness or vomiting blood
Jaundice with severe stomach pain and a high temperature or shivering
urgentFlags: Any new yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Jaundice with dark pee, pale poo or itchy skin
Jaundice in a newborn baby that starts in the first 24 hours or lasts more than 2 weeks

commonCauses.title: Gallstones
commonCauses.detail: A stone blocking the bile duct, often with pain under the right ribs.

commonCauses.title: Hepatitis
commonCauses.detail: Liver inflammation from viruses, alcohol or medicines.

commonCauses.title: Gilbert's syndrome
commonCauses.detail: A common, harmless condition causing mild jaundice during illness or fasting.

commonCauses.title: Pancreatic or liver cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common; often painless jaundice with weight loss.

selfCare: Get medical advice the same day
Avoid alcohol until you have been checked
Make a list of all medicines and supplements you take
avoid: Alcohol
Herbal remedies or supplements that may affect the liver
Taking more paracetamol than the pack allows
seeDoctorIf: You have been told you have mild jaundice before and it comes back often
You have ongoing itchy skin
You are worried about your liver

name: Allergic reaction
summary: Mild allergic reactions cause itching, sneezing or a rash. A severe reaction (anaphylaxis) affects breathing or circulation and is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112).
redFlags: Swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth or throat
Difficulty breathing, wheezing, a hoarse voice or a tight throat
Feeling faint, dizzy, confused or collapsing
Pale, cold or blue-tinged skin, or a fast, weak pulse
Severe reaction after a sting, food or medicine in someone with a known severe allergy
urgentFlags: Swelling of the face or eyes without breathing problems
A widespread itchy rash after a new medicine
Symptoms that are getting worse despite antihistamines

commonCauses.title: Foods
commonCauses.detail: Peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish and sesame are common triggers.

commonCauses.title: Insect stings
commonCauses.detail: Bee and wasp stings.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Antibiotics such as penicillin, anti-inflammatory painkillers and others.

commonCauses.title: Latex, pollen, pets or dust mites
commonCauses.detail: Usually cause milder reactions such as hay fever symptoms or hives.

selfCare: If you have an adrenaline auto-injector, use it at the first signs of a severe reaction and call your local emergency number
Lie down with legs raised if feeling faint, or sit up if struggling to breathe
For mild reactions, ask a pharmacist about antihistamines
Avoid the trigger once identified
avoid: Waiting to see if a severe reaction gets better
Standing up or walking during a severe reaction, even if you feel better
Unproven allergy tests such as hair analysis or applied kinesiology
seeDoctorIf: You have had an allergic reaction and do not know the cause
You have had a severe reaction and do not have an allergy plan or auto-injector
Mild symptoms keep coming back

name: Heat exhaustion
summary: Heat exhaustion causes headache, dizziness, sweating and feeling sick after getting too hot. It should improve within 30 minutes of cooling down; if not, it can turn into heatstroke, which is an emergency.
redFlags: Still unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place and drinking water
A temperature of 40C (104F) or higher, or hot skin that is not sweating
Confusion, fainting, seizures or loss of consciousness
Fast breathing or breathlessness
urgentFlags: Heat symptoms in a baby, young child, older person or someone with a long-term condition
Vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down

commonCauses.title: Hot weather
commonCauses.detail: Especially during heatwaves, and in older people and young children.

commonCauses.title: Exercise or physical work in heat
commonCauses.detail: Without enough rest, shade or fluids.

commonCauses.title: Hot environments
commonCauses.detail: Hot cars, kitchens or rooms without ventilation.

selfCare: Move to a cool place
Lie down and raise the feet slightly
Drink plenty of water, sports drinks or rehydration drinks
Cool the skin with cool water, a wet cloth or a fan; cold packs around the armpits or neck help
avoid: Alcohol and caffeine in hot weather
Exercising in the hottest part of the day
Leaving anyone, especially children or pets, in a parked car
seeDoctorIf: You get heat symptoms easily or often
You take medicines and are unsure if they affect how you cope with heat

name: Feeling very thirsty
summary: Feeling thirsty is normal after exercise, heat or salty food. Being thirsty all the time, especially with peeing a lot, tiredness or weight loss, can be a sign of diabetes.
redFlags: Thirst and peeing a lot with vomiting, stomach pain, deep or fast breathing, breath that smells fruity, or confusion
Extreme thirst with confusion or extreme drowsiness
urgentFlags: Thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss in a child
Thirst with feeling very unwell, dizziness or blurred vision
Thirst with a very high blood sugar reading if you have diabetes

commonCauses.title: Not drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Especially in hot weather or with exercise.

commonCauses.title: Diet
commonCauses.detail: Salty or spicy food and alcohol.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes
commonCauses.detail: High blood sugar causes thirst, peeing a lot, tiredness and weight loss.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines cause a dry mouth or make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, kidney problems or high calcium levels.

selfCare: Drink water regularly through the day
Cut down on salty food, alcohol and sugary drinks
Notice whether you are also peeing more, tired or losing weight
avoid: Quenching thirst with sugary drinks
Ignoring persistent thirst with weight loss
seeDoctorIf: You are always thirsty and peeing a lot
You also feel tired, have blurred vision or have lost weight
You get infections such as thrush or cuts that heal slowly

name: Unexplained weight gain or puffiness
summary: Weight gain is usually linked to diet, activity, medicines or life changes. Rapid weight gain with swelling, or with tiredness and feeling cold, should be checked.
redFlags: Rapid swelling with breathlessness, especially when lying down, or chest pain
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet in pregnancy with severe headache or vision problems
urgentFlags: Gaining a lot of weight over a few days with swollen legs or tummy
Puffiness with peeing much less than usual or foamy pee

commonCauses.title: Diet and activity
commonCauses.detail: Eating more or moving less than usual, including after stopping smoking.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Steroids, some antidepressants, diabetes medicines and others.

commonCauses.title: Underactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Weight gain with tiredness, feeling cold, constipation and dry skin.

commonCauses.title: Fluid retention
commonCauses.detail: Heart, kidney or liver problems can cause rapid weight gain from fluid.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Menopause, polycystic ovary syndrome and, rarely, Cushing's syndrome.

selfCare: Keep a food and activity diary for a couple of weeks
Eat a balanced diet and be active most days
Weigh yourself once a week at the same time
avoid: Crash diets and unregulated weight-loss pills
Stopping a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor
seeDoctorIf: You are gaining weight without a clear reason
You also feel tired, cold or low
You have swelling in your legs or tummy
You think a medicine is causing it
